gaps.concept: The gubernaculum guides testicular descent through the inguinal canal; the accompanying processus vaginalis becomes the tunica vaginalis.
gaps.why_tested: An embryology stem asks which structure guides descent or which peritoneal outpouching accompanies the testis.

gaps.concept: Descending testes acquire external spermatic fascia from external oblique, cremasteric fascia from internal oblique, and internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia.
gaps.why_tested: A labeled inguinal canal diagram asks for the abdominal-wall origin of a spermatic cord covering.

gaps.concept: INSL3 drives transabdominal testicular descent; androgens drive the later inguinoscrotal phase.
gaps.why_tested: A fetal hormone defect is paired with the stage of failed testicular descent.

gaps.concept: Cryptorchid testes show heat-related seminiferous tubular atrophy and impaired germ-cell maturation, often with preserved Leydig cells.
gaps.why_tested: A biopsy or infertility stem asks which testicular compartment is damaged by an undescended testis.

gaps.concept: A patent processus vaginalis can admit bowel or omentum, producing an indirect inguinal hernia rather than a fluid-only hydrocele.
gaps.why_tested: A reducible scrotal swelling with a cough impulse must be distinguished from a communicating hydrocele.

gaps.concept: Spermatic cord torsion first blocks venous outflow, then arterial inflow, causing congestion and hemorrhagic testicular infarction.
gaps.why_tested: A painful testis is followed by a gross pathology image or a question about the sequence of vascular injury.

gaps.concept: Color Doppler shows reduced or absent testicular flow in torsion but increased flow in epididymo-orchitis; pyuria favors infection.
gaps.why_tested: An acute-scrotum stem asks which imaging or urine finding separates ischemia from inflammation.

gaps.concept: Torsion of the appendix testis causes focal upper-pole pain and a blue-dot sign with preserved testicular perfusion.
gaps.why_tested: A prepubertal boy has acute scrotal pain but intact testicular blood flow.

gaps.concept: Tuberculous epididymitis can spread to the testis, producing caseating granulomas, a beaded vas deferens, and obstructive infertility.
gaps.why_tested: A chronic scrotal mass and infertility occur in a patient with tuberculosis exposure.

gaps.concept: A hematocele is blood within the tunica vaginalis after trauma and generally does not transilluminate.
gaps.why_tested: A post-trauma scrotal swelling must be distinguished from a simple hydrocele.

gaps.concept: Testicular rupture tears the tunica albuginea; ultrasound may show a disrupted testicular contour and heterogeneous parenchyma.
gaps.why_tested: A blunt-trauma stem asks for the structure torn or the finding that identifies rupture.

gaps.concept: Testicular cancer usually presents as a painless, firm intratesticular mass; ultrasound typically shows a solid, vascular hypoechoic lesion.
gaps.why_tested: A young man has persistent painless enlargement that must be distinguished from a benign extratesticular cyst.

gaps.concept: Prior testicular germ-cell tumor, family history, infertility, and gonadal dysgenesis increase germ-cell tumor risk.
gaps.why_tested: A risk-factor stem describes a testicular mass without cryptorchidism.

gaps.concept: Classic seminoma has uniform clear cells separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytic infiltrates.
gaps.why_tested: A testicular tumor photomicrograph shows the architecture surrounding fried-egg cells.

gaps.concept: Pure seminoma never elevates AFP; syncytiotrophoblasts can cause a modest β-hCG rise.
gaps.why_tested: Tumor-marker results distinguish pure seminoma from a mixed or nonseminomatous tumor.

gaps.concept: Embryonal carcinoma has primitive pleomorphic cells forming glandular or papillary structures, often with necrosis and early invasion.
gaps.why_tested: A histology image or early-metastasis stem distinguishes embryonal carcinoma from seminoma.

gaps.concept: Yolk sac tumors may contain eosinophilic hyaline globules in addition to Schiller-Duval bodies.
gaps.why_tested: A pediatric testicular tumor biopsy shows AFP-positive globules without a clearly visible Schiller-Duval body.

gaps.concept: Choriocarcinoma contains cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without chorionic villi; a tiny primary can produce hemorrhagic lung or brain metastases.
gaps.why_tested: Hemoptysis or cerebral hemorrhage accompanies a small testicular lesion and markedly elevated β-hCG.

gaps.concept: Teratoma contains tissues from multiple germ layers; prepubertal testicular teratomas are generally benign.
gaps.why_tested: A child’s testicular mass contains cartilage, skin, and glandular tissue, prompting an age-dependent prognosis question.

gaps.concept: Spermatocytic tumor occurs in older men, grows slowly, and lacks the GCNIS and chromosome 12p association of typical adult germ-cell tumors.
gaps.why_tested: An older patient’s indolent testicular tumor must be separated from classic seminoma or lymphoma.

gaps.concept: Sertoli cell tumors form tubules and often stain for inhibin; estrogen-producing variants can cause gynecomastia.
gaps.why_tested: A testicular tumor with tubular histology and feminizing symptoms must be identified as sex cord–stromal.

gaps.concept: Y-chromosome material in dysgenetic gonads predisposes to gonadoblastoma.
gaps.why_tested: A patient with disordered sexual development has a gonadal mass and a Y-containing karyotype.

gaps.concept: Scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes, unlike the testis, which drains to para-aortic nodes.
gaps.why_tested: A lymph-node stem asks whether a lesion arose in scrotal skin or testicular tissue.

gaps.concept: Metastatic nonseminomatous germ-cell tumors are treated with bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin; characteristic toxicities include pulmonary fibrosis, secondary leukemia, and nephrotoxicity.
gaps.why_tested: A chemotherapy vignette asks which drug caused toxicity after treatment for testicular cancer.
